title: Explainer: The CMIP7 emissions scenarios – and how they explore future climate change - Carbon Brief
gist: The seven new CMIP7 emissions scenarios that will underpin the IPCC's seventh assessment cycle narrow projected 2100 warming to 1.6-3.3C from the SSPs' 1.5-4.7C, cutting the high end for the first time in four modelling generations because cheap solar, wind, batteries and a coal plateau make an RCP8.5-style coal century implausible. At the same time the low end has moved up — some overshoot of 1.5C is now treated as unavoidable — and every warming-limiting scenario leans on 655-2,360GtCO2 of cumulative carbon dioxide removal by 2150.

insights.claim: The seven new CMIP7 emissions scenarios span global warming in 2100 of 1.6C to 3.3C above pre-industrial levels, a markedly narrower band than the 1.5C to 4.7C range of their SSP predecessors used in IPCC AR6.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: The official uncertainty band that underwrites climate risk models, TCFD-style disclosures and insurance catastrophe pricing is about to tighten at both ends — high-end tail scenarios used in stress tests will look overstated, and 1.5C-aligned product claims will look harder to defend.

insights.claim: The top of the IPCC scenario range has fallen for the first time in four generations of climate modelling: the highest scenarios in the three previous assessment cycles all produced roughly 4.6-4.9C of warming in 2100, whereas CMIP7's high scenario reaches only 3.3C with around half the cumulative CO2 emissions.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: A structural break in the worst-case anchor: anyone whose thesis depends on catastrophic-warming headlines (adaptation plays, doom-framed ESG products) loses its scientific baseline, while the mid-range physical risk case gets more credible.
insights.locator: The top of the scenario range has fallen

insights.claim: CMIP7's high scenario emits about 3,820GtCO2 cumulatively over 2024-2100 — roughly half the ~7,600GtCO2 of SSP5-8.5 and about three-quarters of the 5,140GtCO2 of SSP3-7.0.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Cumulative CO2 is what drives warming, so this halving is the number to cite when repricing long-dated physical-risk assumptions in infrastructure, real estate and sovereign models.
insights.locator: In cumulative terms – which is what matters most

insights.claim: The most extreme emissions pathway now offered to climate modellers sits, in cumulative terms, between the old SSP2-4.5 and SSP3-7.0 pathways — territory the previous modelling generation treated as its middle ground.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Any model, disclosure or scenario analysis still branding SSP2-4.5 as its 'moderate' case is now effectively running the new worst case — a re-labelling risk for published climate stress tests.
insights.quote: the top of the new scenario range sits between SSP2-4.5 and SSP3-7.0 in cumulative emissions terms, which is territory that CMIP6 treated as its middle ground.
insights.locator: To put it another way

insights.claim: The entire CMIP6 high tier — SSP5-8.5 and SSP3-7.0 — now sits above anything in the new scenario set up to 2100, though the high scenario keeps climbing after 2100 towards levels those extreme scenarios reached earlier.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Extreme warming has been deferred rather than deleted — a signal for very long-duration assets such as coastal property, ice-sheet-linked sea-level exposure and 2100+ liability tails.

insights.claim: Cheap solar, wind and batteries, a global plateau in coal use and more than $2tn per year of clean-energy investment mean that even a full rollback of climate policy would not produce the coal deployment assumed in RCP8.5.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Cost-driven technology lock-in, not policy, is now the binding constraint on the emissions tail — a structural argument that renewables demand is politically resilient even under hostile administrations.

insights.claim: The peer-reviewed Geoscientific Model Development study behind the new scenarios states that the previous generation's high-emission levels have become implausible on the basis of renewables cost trends, the emergence of climate policy and recent emissions trends.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: A formal scientific retirement of the RCP8.5-style worst case removes a rhetorical asset from both climate-alarm and climate-skeptic camps; expect the citation to appear in litigation, disclosure and policy debates.

insights.claim: Only about 0.7C of the roughly 1.7C gap between SSP5-8.5 and today's current-policy trajectory reflects genuine emissions progress; the remainder reflects that the old high-end baseline was never particularly likely in the first place.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Roughly 60% of the celebrated 'avoided warming' is a communication correction, not decarbonisation — a caution against reading the narrower range as evidence that the transition is running ahead of schedule.

insights.claim: The old RCP8.5 scenario produced more 2100 warming (4.9C) than its successor SSP5-8.5 (4.6C) despite lower CO2 emissions, because it assumed considerably more methane and nitrous oxide.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Non-CO2 gas assumptions can swing headline warming by several tenths of a degree — a reminder that methane abatement value is highly sensitive to which scenario generation a model is built on.

insights.claim: CMIP7's high scenario is explicitly built as a plausible rollback of current mitigation policies rather than a no-policy world, meaning that even deliberate policy reversal is now modelled as producing 3.3C rather than near-5C warming.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Political risk to climate policy has a quantified ceiling now — useful for bounding downside scenarios on carbon-price-dependent assets when governments turn hostile.
insights.locator: No more ‘baseline’ scenarios

insights.claim: The new medium scenario, which freezes climate policies officially implemented as of 2025 and assumes no delivery of unlegislated NDCs or net-zero targets, reaches 2.9C of warming in 2100, crossing 2C around 2050 and 3C around 2110.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: This is the closest thing to a market baseline for physical climate risk: near-3C by 2100 with 2C breached inside most infrastructure asset lifetimes.
insights.locator: The medium scenario, by contrast

insights.claim: Under the current-policy medium scenario there is roughly a one-in-four chance of exceeding 4C by 2150, rising to about 50% if emissions continue beyond that date.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: The fat tail has moved from 2100 to 2150 rather than disappearing — relevant to multi-generational liabilities such as sovereign debt, pension liabilities and coastal land value.
insights.locator: The chance of exceeding 4C is around one-in-four

insights.claim: Even the current-policy medium scenario retains roughly a 3% chance of reaching 4C by 2100 and 25% by 2150, an outcome described as far outside anything resembling a safe result for the climate system.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: A narrower scenario range does not mean a benign one; tail-risk hedges tied to extreme warming still have a live, non-trivial probability attached by the official science.
insights.quote: This remains far outside anything resembling a safe outcome for the climate system.
insights.locator: The CMIP7 medium scenario – which has a central estimate

insights.claim: The scenario authors explicitly warn that the medium, current-policy scenario should not be treated as a most-likely forecast, but only as a benchmark against which future policy strengthening or weakening can be measured.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Guards against the common analyst error of treating the middle scenario as an expected value; it is a reference point, and policy drift in either direction is the tradeable variable.
insights.quote: should not be considered as a ‘most likely’ scenario

insights.claim: Under the high scenario, 2C arrives in the 2040s, 3C in the 2080s, the chance of exceeding 4C by 2150 is about 60% and roughly 20% of simulations reach 5C by 2150.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Defines the upper stress-test envelope for adaptation-exposed sectors — water, agriculture, cooling demand and reinsurance — under a policy-rollback world.

insights.claim: A future that avoids any overshoot of 1.5C is no longer considered plausible by the scenario developers, who state that at this point some overshoot of 1.5C seems unavoidable.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: The 1.5C-aligned framing behind trillions in transition finance and corporate targets no longer has a no-overshoot pathway to reference; expect target language to shift towards peak-warming and overshoot-return metrics.
insights.quote: At this point of time, some overshoot of the 1.5C seems unavoidable.
insights.locator: The very-low scenario limits global warming

insights.claim: The very-low scenario peaks at around 1.8C mid-century before falling back close to 1.6C by 2100, and carries roughly a 90% chance that peak warming exceeds 1.5C on the IPCC's 20-year-average convention.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Overshoot-and-return is now the best realistic case, which structurally raises the value of carbon removal capacity and of adaptation for the 2040s-2060s peak window.

insights.claim: The very-low scenario budgets 310GtCO2 of cumulative emissions between 2024 and 2100, nearly three times the roughly 110GtCO2 of its SSP1-1.9 predecessor, reflecting the world's failure to start rapidly cutting emissions after 2020.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Five years of policy delay have quantifiably loosened the ambitious end of the range — evidence that missed near-term abatement gets refinanced as later removal obligations rather than disappearing.
insights.locator: The lowest emissions scenarios now have somewhat higher

insights.claim: The new low scenario lands at essentially the same 2100 warming as its SSP1-2.6 analogue but requires more rapid late-century emissions cuts and greater carbon removal to get there.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Identical temperature outcomes now cost more in abatement and removal — the delay premium shows up as demand for CDR rather than as extra warming.

insights.claim: Every CMIP7 scenario that limits warming leans heavily on carbon dioxide removal, with cumulative removals by 2150 ranging from 655GtCO2 in the very-low scenario to 2,360GtCO2 in the low-to-negative scenario.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: The official climate pathways structurally embed a multi-gigatonne CDR industry that does not yet exist at scale — the clearest top-down demand signal for removal credits, BECCS, DAC and enhanced weathering.
insights.locator: Every scenario that limits warming leans heavily

insights.claim: The low-to-negative scenario pulls a cumulative 2,360GtCO2 from the atmosphere by 2150, described as roughly 60 years of today's emissions run in reverse.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: A vivid scale check on the removal industry's implied build-out; useful for sanity-testing bullish CDR market forecasts against physical feasibility.
insights.quote: roughly 60 years of today’s emissions run in reverse

insights.claim: In the low-to-negative scenario, direct air capture alone reaches around 16GtCO2 per year by 2100, with removals coming almost entirely from engineered rather than land-based methods.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Sets an implied ceiling scale for DAC capacity — orders of magnitude above today's plants — and marks engineered removal, not forestry, as the swing technology in the deepest-cut pathway.
insights.locator: In the low scenario, roughly one-third

insights.claim: The low-to-negative scenario injects roughly 1,750GtCO2 of BECCS and direct-air-capture CO2 underground by 2150, exceeding the prudent geologic storage limit of 1,460GtCO2 set out in Gidden et al. (2025).
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Storage capacity, not capture cost, may be the binding constraint on the deepest mitigation pathway — a bullish signal for non-geologic removal routes and for firms holding proven storage acreage.
insights.locator: The amount of CDR going toward geological storage

insights.claim: The high-to-low and low scenarios each commit around 800GtCO2 to geological storage by 2150, a volume that would require the CO2 storage industry to handle more mass than the fossil-fuel industry currently moves in oil.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Benchmarks the CDR build-out against the largest existing physical logistics business on earth — the implied capex, pipeline and injection-well demand is comparable to global oil midstream.

insights.claim: The volume of carbon removal embedded in these scenarios would require planetary-scale engineering costing trillions of dollars, while many of the engineered removal approaches remain relatively early-stage technologies.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Flags execution risk in the official pathways: warming-limiting scenarios depend on an unproven industry, so scenario-based valuations carry a large embedded technology bet.

insights.claim: Removal approaches that avoid geological injection — enhanced rock weathering, surficial mineralisation, ocean alkalinity enhancement and in-situ mineralisation into basalt or peridotite — are identified as the route around the geologic storage ceiling.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Names the specific technology set that gains relative value if storage capacity binds — a watchlist for early-stage removal ventures and offtake buyers.

insights.claim: Carbon removal is described as one of the few levers available for actually reducing future temperatures, made more necessary by the additional warming caused by cuts to aerosol pollution.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Air-quality progress mechanically raises the removal burden — a second-order link between shipping and industrial pollution rules and CDR demand.

insights.claim: Updated socioeconomic assumptions put the global population peaking at 10.1 billion around 2080 in the medium pathway, with income per person in 2100 running 10-25% lower than in the original SSPs.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: A poorer, more crowded century weakens the assumed self-financing capacity for adaptation and mitigation in developing economies — relevant to climate-finance flows and sovereign risk.
insights.quote: In short, the socioeconomic world underlying the new scenarios is somewhat more crowded and less wealthy per person than the one the SSPs originally imagined.

insights.claim: The updated SSP2 storyline projects 9.9 billion people in 2100, one billion more than the 2013-era version, while GDP was revised down in the high-growth SSP1 and SSP5 storylines.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: More people and less income per head is a directionally bearish input for long-run consumption-driven demand forecasts built on old SSP macro assumptions.
insights.locator: The change in socioeconomic assumptions is substantial

insights.claim: The high-emissions scenario has switched its underlying storyline from the fossil-fuelled-development SSP5 to the fragmented, regional-rivalry SSP3, because modelling teams judged that a fragmented world with large adaptation challenges is now the more relevant way to explore high-end risk.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Geopolitical fragmentation, not a fossil-fuel boom, is now the official channel to worst-case climate outcomes — aligning climate tail risk with deglobalisation and trade-bloc risk factors.

insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: The scenario set is now dominated by trend-continuation macro assumptions, which narrows the diversity of socioeconomic futures analysts can source from official pathways.

themes.theme: Model design changes that shift uncertainty

insights.claim: For the first time, CMIP7 models with an interactive carbon cycle will be run in emissions-driven mode for CO2, calculating atmospheric concentrations themselves rather than being handed prescribed concentrations.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Carbon-cycle feedback uncertainty will now appear directly inside the projected warming range, which is likely to widen published AR7 uncertainty bands even as the emissions range narrows.
insights.locator: First, CMIP7 models will be driven by emissions

insights.claim: Methane, nitrous oxide and halocarbons remain prescribed as concentrations in CMIP7 even though CO2 moves to emissions-driven mode, so only CO2 feedback uncertainty is internalised.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Non-CO2 feedback risk stays outside the headline model spread — a known blind spot when reading AR7 ranges as complete uncertainty.
insights.locator: (The change applies to CO2 only

insights.claim: The new scenarios are harmonised to observed emissions through 2023 and asked to track observed trends to 2025, with scenario divergence only opening up after 2026, fixing the earlier problem of scenarios diverging from reality before the models had even been run.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Near-term projections should track observed data more closely, making the new scenarios more usable for decade-scale planning than the SSPs, which were already stale by the time AR6 concluded.
insights.locator: Second, emissions match observations up to 2023

insights.claim: Model runs are extended from 2100 to 2150, with all scenarios carrying further extensions to 2500 in which temperatures eventually stabilise, allowing exploration of ice sheets, sea level and whether warming is reversible.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Sea-level and reversibility results out to 2500 will become the new evidence base for very long-horizon coastal, insurance and sovereign land-value analysis.
insights.locator: Finally, the period over which models are being run

insights.claim: The CMIP7 authors eliminated no-climate-policy baseline scenarios entirely, so the whole range now starts from current policies and explores strengthening, weakening or continuation.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Removes the counterfactual that companies and governments have long used to claim large avoided-emissions benefits; abatement claims will need a current-policy baseline instead.
insights.locator: In another important change, the authors

insights.claim: The scenario developers assign no likelihood or probability to any of the seven pathways, only a judgement of plausibility, and explicitly acknowledge that potential futures may lie outside the ScenarioMIP range.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Warns against probability-weighting the seven pathways in risk models; the narrower range is a plausibility judgement, not a distribution, and leaves open tails uncovered.
insights.quote: there might be potential futures outside the ScenarioMIP scenario range
insights.locator: The scenario developers noted that there is no specific likelihood

insights.claim: High-level details of the seven CMIP7 scenarios were published in Geoscientific Model Development in April 2026, with the underlying emissions data released into the public domain on 1 September and first model runs already completed in spring 2026 with initial results expected later this year.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: A datable catalyst calendar: first CMIP7 model results land within months and will reset the numbers cited in climate policy, disclosure frameworks and transition-risk models ahead of AR7.
insights.locator: In April 2026, high-level details

insights.claim: Each of the seven scenarios is produced by a different integrated assessment model — GCAM 8s for high, WITCH 6.0 for high-to-low, IMAGE 3.4 for medium, COFFEE 1.6 for medium-low, MESSAGEix-GLOBIOM 2.1 for low, REMIND-MAgPIE for very-low and AIM 3.0 for low-to-negative.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Each pathway carries its own model's technology-cost assumptions, so cross-scenario comparisons of CDR mix or energy build-out partly reflect modelling-team choices rather than physics.

insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: A practical data-pipeline trap: anyone ingesting the raw scenario database for risk modelling will mis-map pathways unless the naming mismatch is handled.

insights.claim: The narrowing of the scenario range is framed as cutting both ways: the implausibility of past worst cases is good news, but the very-low scenarios have simultaneously become harder to achieve because global emissions have yet to decline.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: The correct read is convergence towards a 2-3C world rather than either catastrophe or success — which favours adaptation and resilience exposure over both doom and 1.5C-purity narratives.
